title: Request for a Corrosion-Resistant Cabin Floor Seat Track Standard for Returning Lease Aircraft
abstract: Lessor asks for a durable seat track standard after finding heavy corrosion in the galley and lavatory runs on every aircraft coming back from a first lease, driving unplanned redelivery work and dispute with the outgoing operator.

sections.request: We have taken back eleven aircraft of this family in the last two years and on every single one the floor under the forward galley and around the aft lavatories has needed track work before we could place the aircraft with the next operator. It is always the same picture: the anodising has gone, the track is pitted along the fastener line and the seat fittings will not lock reliably. The repair is slow because the cabin has to come out, and it lands on us because the outgoing operator argues that spillage is normal wear. What we want is a track that survives fifteen years of galley and lavatory spillage without needing to be cut out, so that a redelivery is a cabin refresh and not a structural job.
sections.background: Redelivery inspections since 2024 have produced an average of nineteen metres of track replacement per aircraft, and on two aircraft the floor panel support angles beneath the track also had to be renewed. Our engineering department has trialled a barrier sealant applied at cabin refresh, which delayed the problem but did not stop it. The existing published repair is a splice, which is acceptable once but cannot be repeated at the same station, so aircraft on their second lease are reaching a point where the whole run has to be replaced.
sections.expected_outcome: A seat track that can be installed at a normal cabin refresh, that does not need the floor beams to be modified, and that survives a full lease term in a wet cabin zone without corrosion. We would also like a clear position on how many splices a run can carry before it must be replaced entirely.

type_data.business_justification: Track replacement at redelivery is costing between 210 and 340 thousand euros per aircraft and holds the asset out of revenue for nine to fourteen days beyond the planned transition. Over a portfolio of forty-one aircraft approaching first lease end, the lessor values the exposure at more than eleven million euros.
